title: Ryan McClead on Writing With Claude and What AI Agents Mean for Legal Work
author: Ryan McClead

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The excerpt only provides information on obtaining a free PDF or printed copy. It offers no substantive claim about organisational adaptation, human control, employment, pricing, training or legal AI’s effects, so its position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: McClead concretely develops the cluster’s institutional-knowledge proposition by explaining how firms could structure expertise for AI retrieval and execution. His proposed mechanism could make firm-designed workflows available by default while preserving user override, although it is illustrated rather than empirically validated and does not resolve broader succession or competence-development questions.
qs: And I think that, for me, was the aha moment as I was working through this, that the opportunity for KM and innovation teams is to do what they’ve been doing, but rather than focusing entirely on getting the knowledge in a format and structure that is easily findable, readable, and usable by people, get the knowledge in a structure that is findable, readable, and usable by the AI, as well as people.

Whereas now, the AI can make it usable and executable in a way that it’s going to do the workflow the way that you’ve designed, unless it’s actively overwritten by somebody, without that person needing to be trained or knowing exactly what the steps are or things like that.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: McClead accepts the cluster’s core view that AI selectively accelerates rather than replaces expert legal work, with human judgment remaining essential. He materially extends it by proposing executable knowledge workflows, bounded AI workspaces and purpose-built deterministic tools for tasks requiring exact, repeatable language.
qs: The person with the knowledge, with the understanding, with the judgment is absolutely imperative, right?
But if you want to get the exact right language that you use for this thing every time, you don’t use a probabilistic engine.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s caution against treating product-usage signals as direct evidence of realized value. Her account says Harvey’s rising token consumption reflects both increased adoption and greater product complexity, making token use an ambiguous indicator rather than a standalone measure of uptake or economic benefit.
qs: Nikki Shaver (01:07)  But he also talked about very interesting developments, for example, the escalating token use within the Harvey product, indicating increased adoption, but also the drain on tokens from the increased complexity of the product.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: McClead’s firsthand account supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between context-aware assistance and autonomous practice: project context simplifies collaborative drafting, but the output still requires detailed human editorial review. Its evidentiary value is limited because the example concerns blog writing rather than legal workflows and does not address whether specialist legal procedure protects specialist vendors.
qs: But when you have all these rules files and you have the memories that Claude creates on its own, or that you tell it to create, that are again tied strictly to the project, all of that context gets pulled in when it needs to.
But then I had to go through line by line and say, no, I wouldn’t say that.

kp.k: Harvey usage reflects adoption and increasing product complexity
kp.d: Reporting on Harvey Forum, Nikki Shaver says CEO Winston Weinberg described escalating token use as reflecting both increased adoption and more complex product functionality; no usage figures are provided. She also reports the launch of Command Center for usage management and reporting, and a Harvey–DeepJudge relationship providing access within Harvey to research across multiple systems’ data.
qs: the escalating token use within the Harvey product, indicating increased adoption, but also the drain on tokens from the increased complexity of the product.
Harvey also launched Command Center, which is a way that firms can now manage and track usage and get much clearer reporting to help them drive adoption.
He also announced a relationship between Harvey and DeepJudge that will give DeepJudge users access to DeepJudge’s legal research across multiple systems’ data in the Harvey system

kp.k: Transformation value extends beyond efficiency gains
kp.d: Shaver reports that her forum panel discussed assessing law-firm transformation ROI through differentiation grounded in expertise and data, rather than efficiency alone. This is an account of a panel’s framing, not a measured finding about financial returns.
qs: we really dug into what it means for law firms to look at ROI in terms of value, not just from efficiency gains, but also from the ability to differentiate and focus on what a firm’s superpower is from an expertise perspective and a data perspective.

kp.k: AI drafting shifts work toward selection and revision
kp.d: McClead describes an autobiographical experiment rather than a legal-work productivity study: Claude agents produced 79,000 words across 19 chapters, which he judged poor and partly irrelevant to his clients. He cut the material to approximately the eventual length within a day, then worked through revisions over five weeks. He characterises the shift as replacing blank-page drafting with substantial human focusing, editing and collaboration, not producing a finished book automatically.
qs: It spit out 79,000 words. Yeah, it was 19 chapters.
Reading a little bit more, I’m like, okay, this is terrible.
So it inverts the writing process in an interesting way, but I’m not staring at a blank page anymore, and that’s fascinating.
it was five weeks of solid work.

kp.k: Expert judgment remains essential despite task delegation
kp.d: McClead interprets his experience as supporting augmentation rather than replacement: AI may perform work without eliminating the person responsible for knowledge and judgment. He warns against replacing first-year associates with AI and argues that greater existing competence enables greater benefit. These are practitioner judgments, not demonstrated employment effects.
qs: the AI that’s going to do your job is not the one that’s going to replace you. At least that’s not how I see it, having done it.
The person with the knowledge, with the understanding, with the judgment is absolutely imperative, right?
If you fire a bunch of people and say, we’re going to have AI do this instead of first-year associates, that’s not going to be good for anybody.
These tools, the better you are at something, the better they will make you, the faster they will allow you to do these sorts of things.

kp.k: Knowledge management can become executable through AI skills
kp.d: McClead proposes that KM and innovation teams structure knowledge for AI as well as human discovery and use. Firm-developed skills could then be selected by the AI and execute intended workflows without users knowing that a skill exists or learning its steps. He notes that users can bypass the skill, so the mechanism does not guarantee adherence.
qs: rather than focusing entirely on getting the knowledge in a format and structure that is easily findable, readable, and usable by people, get the knowledge in a structure that is findable, readable, and usable by the AI, as well as people.
They don’t even need to know that the skill exists.
You need to build the skill in a way that the AI knows it’s available and it can be used.

it’s going to do the workflow the way that you’ve designed, unless it’s actively overwritten by somebody, without that person needing to be trained or knowing exactly what the steps are or things like that.

kp.k: Clients may request executable tools instead of memoranda
kp.d: As a single recent client anecdote, McClead reports that a client not deploying Claude contacted him two days earlier because its corporate client requested a Claude skill rather than a regulatory memo. He says he built a workspace enabling a lawyer to insert regulatory expertise and package it for the corporate client’s use. He presents this as a new way to deliver consultant and lawyer knowledge, while acknowledging implementation problems.
qs: I had a client contact me two days ago, a client who’s not deploying Claude at the moment, saying that their corporate client has asked for a Claude skill.
Not, I want a memo explaining this regulation. I want a Claude skill that my team can use to do this thing.
I built the skill in such a way that the lawyer can use it to put their own knowledge and understanding of the regulation in
That is my knowledge that I’ve made executable for my clients in such a way that they can make it theirs and make it executable for their client.

kp.k: Firm-wide scaling and security remain unresolved
kp.d: Asked by the hosts about poor data, document management, security and scalability, McClead explicitly says he lacks answers and does not dismiss those challenges. He speculates that Microsoft delivery could change the infrastructure and integration options through existing enterprise relationships, but says he has not tried the Microsoft version and does not know its eventual licensing.
qs: And those are all very real challenges, and I’m not dismissing them at all. They need to be addressed. We need to figure them out. I don’t have answers for that.
I think the Microsoft Copilot version, I haven’t played with it yet
that changes some of the infrastructure on the back end, as well as having it delivered via an organization you already have a large contract with, right?
I don’t know what exactly their licensing is going to be or how that’s going to change

kp.k: Begin adoption with small, low-risk experiential pilots
kp.d: McClead recommends starting in an innocuous area where mistakes can cause as little damage as possible, and learning how the tool works through direct experience. He frames this as an established technology-deployment principle rather than a new rule specific to agents.
qs: The first step is always start small. Start small in an innocuous area that’s going to do as little damage as possible.
That’s true of any technology you deploy.
In this case, I think the first thing you need to do is experience it.

kp.k: Persistent context shifts interaction from prompting to delegation
kp.d: McClead argues that agentic workspaces reduce the need to specify every instruction afresh: project files, personal, project and enterprise rules, and project memories supply context. He regards prompting as lacking durability as a distinct skill, while qualifying that prompting knowledge remains useful and the underlying model mechanics have not changed. His writing example places human effort in developing concepts and editing outputs rather than composing each next word.
qs: Prompting is not a skill that has durability, I don’t think.
Not that it’s not important and not that it’s not useful. It is still good to know because technically the tools still work exactly the same way. The difference is you don’t have to do all of that.
Each project has its own rules file. The enterprise has a rules file. Those automatically get pulled in for each project every time.
I spent my time thinking about the underlying concepts and the points that I wanted to make.

kp.k: Rules and workspace boundaries require distinct safeguards
kp.d: McClead cautions that enterprise instructions remain probabilistic rather than ironclad. Separately, he describes limiting a project’s accessible material through a defined workspace, suggests a second read-only folder for some information, and distinguishes tool-mediated database retrieval from crawling an entire database. These are his descriptions and recommendations for workspace configuration, not evidence that firm-wide governance problems have been solved.
qs: So whatever the firm has set as sacrosanct is, keep in mind, still probabilistic. So it’s not ironclad that it’s going to do something or not do something
I talk at one point in the book about the potential for using a second read-only folder.
You tell it, this is your workspace. This is where you can work. It doesn’t have access to anything else, only what you give it.
But it doesn’t crawl the entire database.

kp.k: Verify model explanations and actively direct collaboration
kp.d: McClead recounts Claude incorrectly explaining its own memory operation and proposing to rewrite a chapter; he stopped it and checked documentation. He also warns against passive assent, describes configuring the tool to challenge him, and recommends defining completion criteria to avoid endless iteration and diminishing returns. These lessons arise from his writing experience.
qs: One of the things to keep in mind is never trust that the tool works the way the tool says it does.
I went through all of the documentation. Okay, that is not true. Here’s how it works, right?
You have to be deliberate about what you’re doing and what you’re telling it to do.
Because the AI will iterate forever. And there’s a point of diminishing returns.

kp.k: Exact legal language still warrants purpose-built automation
kp.d: McClead distinguishes tolerable imperfections in his book from the requirements of contract drafting. He argues that probabilistic generation does not replace document automation when the same exact language is required every time, although it can assist parts of that process. He leaves future changes uncertain and maintains a role for purpose-built tools.
qs: It’s a different thing if you’re writing a contract.
This doesn’t replace document automation. It can help you with certain aspects of document automation.
But if you want to get the exact right language that you use for this thing every time, you don’t use a probabilistic engine.
So there is a need for purpose-built tools beyond these tools.

kp.k: Conversational agents are predicted to become the working model
kp.d: In his explicitly forward-looking answer, McClead predicts that conversational delegation will shape future work regardless of which product prevails. Users would direct desired outcomes while the tool handles intermediate steps rather than requiring manually chained prompts. He recommends asking the agent to ask clarifying questions to elicit relevant information the user has not supplied, and says agents sometimes find better methods than those users would prescribe.
qs: I don’t know that this is the tool that we’re going to use going forward. But I think this is the model.
It’s about having a tool that you can converse with in a normal-language sort of way, conversationally, and have it do things on your behalf that you’re directing and creating outputs, right?
just say, ask me any questions.
And in whatever form that takes, whatever product that ends up being, that’s the way we’re going to work.
It often finds a better way to do something than you would have told it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McClead predicts that conversational delegation to agents, rather than detailed prompting and manually sequenced workflows, will become the working model.
pts.d: McClead distinguishes the emerging mode of work from any particular vendor: users describe objectives conversationally, agents draw on project context and ask clarifying questions, and the tools execute intermediate steps. He argues that prompting is not a durable specialist skill, while qualifying that understanding prompting remains useful because the underlying technology has not fundamentally changed.

pts.k: McClead frames agents as amplifiers of human expertise rather than replacements for knowledgeable legal professionals.
pts.d: Despite his book’s provocative subtitle, McClead says AI doing aspects of a job does not mean replacing its holder. He asserts that knowledge and judgment remain essential and warns against replacing first-year associates with AI. This is his experience-based interpretation, not a measured employment forecast.

pts.k: McClead argues that knowledge management can shift from making knowledge discoverable by people to making it executable by AI.
pts.d: Firm knowledge can be packaged into skills that an agent selects and uses when relevant, without users first knowing that the skill exists or learning its workflow. He presents this as a new route to distributing and applying institutional knowledge, not as guaranteed compliance: users can override skills, and later discussion qualifies the reliability of rules.

pts.k: McClead reports an emerging legal deliverable: reusable AI skills instead of conventional explanatory memoranda.
pts.d: He describes one consulting client whose corporate client requested a Claude skill. McClead says he created a workspace through which a lawyer could supply regulatory expertise and package it for the corporate client to use. He interprets this as executable knowledge passing from consultant to lawyer to client, and as a reason firms must understand these tools even if they have not deployed them.

pts.k: McClead’s writing experience illustrates a shift from producing initial drafts to directing, selecting and refining abundant AI output.
pts.d: In the adjacent domain of professional writing, agents generated a 79,000-word, 19-chapter draft, which McClead judged poor and substantially cut. He reports completing the book in five weeks, something he says he could not have done without Claude, but stresses extensive human work and mixed quality relative to writing alone. He suggests this experience is relevant to possible law-firm workflows without presenting it as a legal productivity benchmark.

pts.k: McClead says probabilistic agents do not eliminate the need for purpose-built document automation.
pts.d: He distinguishes acceptable imperfections in his book from exact-language requirements in contracts. Agents may assist document automation, but he argues that probabilistic generation is unsuitable when identical approved language must be reproduced reliably. He leaves open whether this limitation will change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is McClead’s hands-on experimentation, writing experience and one client engagement, rather than systematic legal-sector measurement.
pts.d: McClead developed his account while using Claude Cowork to understand it for clients and to write a guide that became a book. His examples include iterative drafting, creating a voice profile, constructing a client-facing skill and correcting the tool’s inaccurate explanation of its own memory behavior by consulting documentation. The transcript supplies no controlled comparisons, legal-work accuracy benchmarks, quantified firm ROI, employment data or evidence of enterprise-wide deployment. The five-week writing period and initial draft size describe one project, not general productivity rates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: McClead describes current capabilities and early demand in the 2026 interview, but gives no timetable for widespread adoption.
pts.d: The client request occurred two days before the interview; the book emerged from five weeks of work. The prediction that conversational agents will become the normal working model is undated, and McClead does not commit to Claude as the eventual product. He anticipates more tools and speculates that a Microsoft implementation could alter infrastructure and integration options, while explicitly saying he has not tried it and does not know its outcome or licensing.

pts.k: The proposed changes depend on bounded context, knowledgeable supervision and unresolved enterprise implementation work.
pts.d: McClead acknowledges that poor data, document-management integration, security and scaling remain real challenges for which he has no complete solution. He recommends low-risk experimentation, carefully scoped project access, deliberate direction and clear stopping criteria. Enterprise rules remain probabilistic rather than ironclad. His position therefore concerns what agents make possible, not a claim that secure, maintainable deployment across large firms is already solved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are law-firm KM and innovation teams, lawyers, legal-services consultants and corporate client teams.
pts.d: KM and innovation teams would structure institutional expertise for machine use as well as human retrieval. Lawyers would direct and check agent work, contribute expertise to reusable skills and potentially deliver operational tools rather than only memoranda. Consultants could package methods for lawyers to adapt and redistribute. Corporate clients would use those packages within their own teams. First-year associates appear specifically in McClead’s warning against substitution. Large firms face implementation constraints; the transcript does not establish differential outcomes by firm size, changes to fees or staffing ratios, or access-to-justice effects.
